applied.fact: Difficulty billing of the rock step
Difficulty billing of the rock step

before.best_season: Best June through September; snow often lingers in the connecting basin below Ellinor into early summer, so carry an ice axe (and consider crampons) even though most of the traverse is rock.

before.beta: The traverse is 7 roped pitches (statically belayed, though simulclimbing is possible): fourth-class scrambling to a notch near 6,100 ft, a descent on steep snow into the Great Basin, moderate snow pitches on the east ridge, a sparsely protected rock traverse on the west side, mixed rock-and-snow sections with moat belays, and a final steep couloir ascent to the South Brother summit. The route is recommended north-to-south.

itinerary.cal: The South Couloir often holds snow (ice axe/crampons recommended) into mid-summer and typically melts out to a class 3-4 scramble by late August.

days.note: From the Lena Lake trailhead (~700 ft), a mellow, well-graded trail climbs past Lena Lake and up the Valley of the Silent Men to a forested camp (Lena Forks / East Lena Creek Basin area, ~3,600 ft) at the base of the upper valley. Route-finding gets trickier through the old burn area — carry a GPS track, as the pink flagging is easy to miss.
days.title: Hike in to high camp
days.objective: Reach camp in the Valley of the Silent Men

days.note: An alpine start from camp with light packs to the base of the South Couloir (the second gully from climber's right), then a steep snow/scree climb of roughly 3,000 ft to the summit ridge with a few exposed class 3-4 moves near the top. After summiting, reverse the couloir back to camp, break camp, and hike the full ~6 miles back out to the trailhead the same day — a long second day, but this is how most 2-day parties run it.
days.title: Summit push and hike out

schedule.label: Leave high camp
schedule.detail: Light alpine-start packs; axe/crampons useful if the couloir still holds snow

schedule.label: Reach base of South Couloir
schedule.detail: Short climb up-valley from camp to the gully entrance

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: South (true) summit, 6,866 ft, via the couloir and a short, exposed class 3-4 finish

schedule.label: Back at camp
schedule.detail: Break down camp and repack for the hike out

schedule.label: Reach trailhead
schedule.detail: Round trip from camp back to car; full car-to-car trip runs ~10-11 hrs on summit day

days.objective: Climb the South Couloir to the summit, then pack all the way out

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day trip is the standard way parties do it: hike in ~6 mi to a camp in the Valley of the Silent Men (~2,900 ft gain), then a big second day climbing the South Couloir to the summit and packing all the way back out (~11 mi, ~3,200 ft up / 6,100 ft down). Very fit parties skip the camp and do the whole route car-to-car in a single ~10.5 hr day.

before.watch_out:
Morning snow in couloir can be firm or icy and masks how technical the underlying rock actually is—assess and re-assess snow conditions; if rock climbing is required, retreat if not capable; snow/ice transition can be slippery and dangerous
Crux rock step (20-50 ft above saddle) more serious than Class 3-4 billing suggests—at least one party ended up roping up and placing gear due to steepness and poor rock quality; secure ropes on this section unless climbing with extreme confidence
Don't glissade descent chute without clear sightline to runout—nearby terrain has close calls from parties glissading blind into rocks or drop-offs; walking descent safer than sliding in poor visibility
Couloir/gully approach terrain—potential for rockfall from upper sections; stay compact and move through quickly; afternoon rockfall increase from sun warming; start early
Snow conditions seasonal and highly variable—July-September is the usual window; summer dry conditions expose loose rock; winter requires mountaineering skills; verify current conditions
Route-finding complexity on initial scramble approach—establish correct line before committing; terrain can look similar but lead to worse ground
Moat crossing potential at upper couloir sections—bergschrund may be significant; assess before committing; belay if uncertain
Fatigue on descent—long day with technical climbing can leave climbers tired; descents often cause more injuries; maintain focus and move deliberately on all scrambling
before.bail: The crux rock step above the saddle can be downclimbed carefully, or protected/rappelled off a small nut or sling anchor if it feels too exposed to solo — worth carrying a light rack even though the route is nominally unroped Class 3-4.
